## Task 1: Data Acquisition

```{r}
#| label: acquire-netflix-data

#' Acquiring and Standardizing Netflix What We Watched Reports
#'
#' In this section, I am developing a reproducible data acquisition
#' function to retrieve, consolidate, and standardize Netflix's
#' publicly available "What We Watched" engagement reports.
#'
#' My objective is to construct a comprehensive longitudinal dataset
#' that facilitates the examination of Netflix viewing patterns
#' across successive semiannual reporting periods.
#'
#' Rather than manually downloading individual Excel files, I am
#' implementing an automated retrieval process that identifies
#' the relevant download links directly from Netflix's official
#' publication pages.
#'
#' This approach is particularly important because Netflix distributes
#' its reports through a Content Delivery Network (CDN), where file
#' URLs may contain dynamically generated identifiers.
#'
#' Following acquisition, I am integrating the individual datasets,
#' standardizing temporal variables, addressing missing observations,
#' and transforming relevant attributes into analytically useful formats.


load_netflix_data <- function() {

  # Loading the libraries required for my data acquisition workflow.
  #
  # I am using tidyverse for data manipulation, transformation,
  # and functional programming operations.
  #
  # I am incorporating rvest to extract Excel download links
  # from Netflix's official publication webpages.
  #
  # I am using readxl to import the Excel reports, while fs
  # provides consistent file-system and directory management.

  library(tidyverse)
  library(rvest)
  library(readxl)
  library(fs)


  # Establishing a dedicated directory for my Netflix source files.
  #
  # I am organizing the downloaded reports within data/mp01
  # to maintain a structured and reproducible project environment.
  #
  # Before proceeding, I am checking whether this directory exists.
  # If it does not, I am creating it automatically to prevent
  # file-storage errors during subsequent downloads.

  data_dir <- path("data", "mp01")

  if (!dir_exists(data_dir)) {
    dir_create(
      data_dir,
      showWarnings = FALSE,
      recurse = TRUE
    )
  }


  # Identifying the official Netflix engagement report webpages.
  #
  # I am constructing a named list containing the publication URLs
  # corresponding to each semiannual reporting period.
  #
  # By explicitly associating each URL with its reporting period,
  # I am preserving the temporal provenance of every observation.
  #
  # This structure will subsequently enable me to investigate
  # changes in audience engagement across reporting periods,
  # rather than relying exclusively on aggregated viewing totals.

  NETFLIX_URLS <- list(
    `2023H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-a-netflix-engagement-report",
    `2023H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2023",
    `2024H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2024",
    `2024H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2024",
    `2025H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2025",
    `2025H2` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-second-half-of-2025",
    `2026H1` = "https://about.netflix.com/news/what-we-watched-the-first-half-of-2026"
  )


  # Developing a conditional file-download function.
  #
  # I am implementing this helper function to avoid downloading
  # files that are already available in my local project directory.
  #
  # Specifically, I am checking whether the destination file exists
  # before initiating a download.
  #
  # This conditional approach minimizes redundant network requests,
  # improves computational efficiency, and supports reproducibility
  # when I rerun my analysis.
  #
  # I am also specifying binary download mode to preserve
  # the integrity of the Excel files.

  download_if_needed <- function(url, local) {

    if (!file_exists(local)) {
      download.file(
        url,
        local,
        quiet = TRUE,
        mode = "wb"
      )
    }

    return(local)
  }


  # Extracting the Excel download links from Netflix's webpages.
  #
  # I am iterating over the publication URLs and reading their
  # underlying HTML content using read_html().
  #
  # Because the Excel files are not referenced through fixed URLs,
  # I am using an XPath expression to identify hyperlinks
  # containing the .xlsx file extension.
  #
  # I am subsequently extracting the hyperlink destinations
  # and organizing them into a structured dataset containing
  # the reporting period and corresponding download URL.

  NETFLIX_URLS |>
    map(read_html) |>
    map(
      html_element,
      xpath = "//a[contains(@href, '.xlsx')]"
    ) |>
    map_chr(html_attr, "href") |>
    enframe("period", "url") |>


    # Downloading and importing the semiannual Excel reports.
    #
    # I am generating a standardized local filename for each
    # reporting period and downloading the corresponding file
    # only when it is not already stored locally.
    #
    # Afterward, I am importing each Excel workbook using read_excel().
    #
    # I am skipping the first three rows because they contain
    # preliminary report information rather than the analytical
    # observations required for my investigation.
    #
    # I am also interpreting asterisks as missing values during
    # import and converting release dates into R's Date format.

    mutate(
      path = path(data_dir, paste0(period, ".xlsx")),

      path = map2(
        url,
        path,
        download_if_needed
      ),

      data = map(
        path,
        read_excel,
        skip = 3,
        na = "*"
      ),

      data = map(
        data,
        \(x) x |>
          mutate(
            `Release Date` = as.Date(`Release Date`)
          )
      )
    ) |>


    # Consolidating the individual reporting-period datasets.
    #
    # I am vertically combining the imported reports into
    # one unified dataset using unnest().
    #
    # This consolidation allows me to analyze viewing behavior
    # across multiple reporting periods within a consistent
    # analytical framework.
    #
    # I am removing the temporary URL and file-path columns
    # because they are no longer necessary for subsequent analysis.

    unnest(data) |>
    select(-url, -path) |>


    # Constructing standardized temporal variables.
    #
    # I am extracting the calendar year and reporting half
    # from the period identifier.
    #
    # I am then generating explicit beginning and ending dates
    # for each six-month reporting interval.
    #
    # These variables are essential for examining longitudinal
    # patterns, comparing reporting periods, and identifying
    # changes in Netflix audience engagement over time.

    mutate(
      year = str_sub(period, 1, 4),

      half = str_sub(period, start = 6),

      period_start = make_date(
        year,
        if_else(half == 1, 1, 7),
        1
      ),

      period_end = make_date(
        year,
        if_else(half == 1, 6, 12),
        if_else(half == 1, 30, 31)
      )
    ) |>


    # Removing observations without recorded viewing hours.
    #
    # I am excluding records where Hours Viewed is missing
    # because this variable represents a fundamental measure
    # of audience engagement in my analysis.
    #
    # Retaining observations without this information would
    # limit the interpretability of subsequent calculations
    # involving viewing intensity and content popularity.

    filter(!is.na(`Hours Viewed`)) |>


    # Identifying live events and standardizing content runtime.
    #
    # I am distinguishing live-event programming by detecting
    # runtime values containing an asterisk following a
    # time-formatted expression.
    #
    # I am then removing the asterisk and converting runtime
    # from hours-and-minutes notation into total minutes.
    #
    # This transformation establishes a consistent numerical
    # measure of content duration, which I can subsequently
    # use to investigate viewing preferences for shorter
    # versus longer programming.

    mutate(
      live_event = !is.na(Runtime) &
        str_detect(Runtime, "\\d+:\\d+\\*"),

      clean_time = str_remove(
        Runtime,
        fixed("*")
      ),

      Runtime = 60 * hour(hm(clean_time)) +
        minute(hm(clean_time))
    ) |>


    # Removing the intermediate runtime transformation variable.
    #
    # I am retaining the standardized numerical runtime
    # while eliminating the temporary character-based field
    # used during the conversion process.

    select(-clean_time) |>


    # Addressing missing runtime values and standardizing titles.
    #
    # I am replacing missing runtime observations with the
    # average available runtime for the corresponding title.
    #
    # By performing this calculation within each title,
    # I am attempting to preserve title-specific characteristics
    # rather than substituting a single overall dataset average.
    #
    # I am also normalizing title text by transliterating
    # accented characters into their closest ASCII equivalents.
    #
    # Additionally, I am removing supplementary title information,
    # unsupported trailing characters, and unnecessary whitespace.
    #
    # These transformations help reduce inconsistencies that
    # could otherwise interfere with grouping, comparisons,
    # and identification of recurring titles.

    mutate(
      Runtime = coalesce(
        Runtime,
        mean(Runtime, na.rm = TRUE)
      ),

      .by = Title,

      Title = stringi::stri_trans_general(
        Title,
        "Latin-ASCII"
      ),

      Title = str_remove(
        Title,
        " // .*"
      ),

      Title = str_remove(
        Title,
        "[^[:ascii:]].*"
      ),

      Title = str_trim(Title)
    ) |>


    # Excluding records with empty content titles.
    #
    # I am removing observations that no longer contain
    # a valid title after the standardization process.
    #
    # This ensures that my analytical dataset retains
    # identifiable content records for subsequent comparisons.

    filter_out(Title == "") |>


    # Selecting and organizing the final analytical variables.
    #
    # I am retaining the variables most relevant to my
    # investigation of Netflix engagement patterns.
    #
    # These include reporting periods, content titles,
    # runtime, views, total viewing hours, release dates,
    # global availability, and live-event classification.
    #
    # I am also arranging the columns into a logical order
    # to improve readability and facilitate downstream
    # exploratory analysis and visualization.

    select(
      year,
      period,
      period_start,
      period_end,
      Title,
      -half,
      Runtime,
      Views,
      `Hours Viewed`,
      `Release Date`,
      `Available Globally?`,
      live_event
    )
}


# Executing my Netflix data acquisition function.
#
# I am calling load_netflix_data() to retrieve and process
# the engagement reports into a consolidated dataset.
#
# I am assigning the resulting dataset to NETFLIX_DATA,
# which will serve as the primary analytical foundation
# for the subsequent stages of my mini-project.
#
# By centralizing the acquisition and cleaning operations
# within a single function, I am making my workflow
# more transparent, reproducible, and easier to maintain.

NETFLIX_DATA <- load_netflix_data()
```

## Task 2: Fixing Column Titles

```{r}
#| label: clean-column-names

# Standardizing Netflix Dataset Column Names
#
# In this section, I am standardizing the column names in my
# NETFLIX_DATA dataset to establish a consistent naming convention
# for subsequent data manipulation and analytical procedures.
#
# I am using the rename() function from dplyr to convert the
# original Netflix variable names into lowercase snake_case format.
#
# Specifically, I am replacing spaces with underscores and
# eliminating inconsistent capitalization to improve readability,
# simplify variable referencing, and minimize potential errors
# during subsequent transformations.
#
# I am retaining the original data values and observations,
# ensuring that this operation exclusively modifies the
# nomenclature rather than the substantive dataset.
#
# This standardization will facilitate more efficient data
# exploration, statistical computations, and visualizations
# throughout the remaining stages of my mini-project.

NETFLIX_DATA <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  rename(
    title = Title,
    runtime = Runtime,
    views = Views,
    hours_viewed = `Hours Viewed`,
    release_date = `Release Date`,
    available_globally = `Available Globally?`
  )
```

## Task 3: Fixing Column Types

```{r}
#| label: clean-column-types

# Standardizing Data Types for Analytical Consistency
#
# In this section, I am refining the data types of selected
# variables within my NETFLIX_DATA dataset to ensure consistency,
# computational accuracy, and compatibility with subsequent
# statistical analyses and visualizations.
#
# I am using the mutate() function from dplyr to transform
# variables into data types that appropriately reflect their
# underlying analytical meaning.
#
# First, I am converting the year variable into an integer
# using as.integer(). This transformation ensures that the
# reporting year is represented numerically rather than as
# a character string, facilitating chronological comparisons,
# temporal aggregations, and longitudinal trend analysis.
#
# Second, I am transforming the available_globally variable
# into a logical (Boolean) indicator by evaluating whether
# its original value equals "Yes".
#
# Under this transformation, titles designated as globally
# available are assigned TRUE, while those with other
# nonmissing values are assigned FALSE. Missing values
# remain NA, preserving uncertainty in the original data.
#
# This binary classification will allow me to distinguish
# between globally available and geographically restricted
# content when examining differences in audience engagement.
#
# By explicitly standardizing these variable types, I am
# strengthening the structural integrity of my dataset,
# reducing potential inconsistencies, and establishing
# a more reliable foundation for subsequent analytical tasks.
#
# Finally, I am updating NETFLIX_DATA with these transformations
# while preserving all other variables and observations.

NETFLIX_DATA <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(year),
    available_globally = available_globally == "Yes"
  )
```

## Task 4: Initial Exploratory Data Analysis

### Dataset Structure and Variable Types

```{r}
#| label: task4-glimpse

# Examining the Structure and Composition of My Netflix Dataset
#
# In this section, I am conducting a preliminary structural
# examination of my cleaned and standardized NETFLIX_DATA dataset
# to assess its overall organization and analytical readiness.
#
# I am using the glimpse() function from dplyr to obtain a
# concise overview of the dataset, including its dimensions,
# variable names, data types, and representative observations.
#
# Specifically, I am verifying that the column names conform

#
# I am also examining the number of observations and variables
# to better understand the scope and dimensionality of the
# consolidated Netflix engagement reports.
#
# This preliminary inspection allows me to identify potential
# structural inconsistencies, unexpected variable types,
# or missing values that may warrant further investigation.
#
# By validating the structure of my dataset before proceeding,
# I am establishing a foundation for subsequent exploratory

#
# Ultimately, this step serves as an initial quality-assurance

# and preprocessing procedures have produced a coherent

glimpse(NETFLIX_DATA)
```

### Descriptive Summary Statistics

```{r}
#| label: task4-skim

# Conducting a Comprehensive Exploratory Assessment of My Netflix Dataset
#
# In this section, I am extending my preliminary structural
# inspection by conducting a more comprehensive examination
# of the statistical characteristics and data quality of
# my cleaned and standardized NETFLIX_DATA dataset.
#
# I am loading the skimr package, which provides a systematic
# framework for generating descriptive summaries across
# multiple variable types within a single dataset.
#
# Unlike glimpse(), which primarily examines the structural
# composition of my data, skim() enables me to investigate
# the distributional properties, completeness, and statistical
# characteristics of individual variables.
#
# Specifically, I am examining the number of missing observations,
# the proportion of complete records, and the distinct values
# associated with relevant categorical variables.
#
# For numerical variables such as runtime, views, and hours_viewed,
# I am evaluating descriptive statistics, including measures
# of central tendency, dispersion, and distributional variation.
#
# These summaries will help me identify potentially anomalous
# observations, substantial differences in viewing engagement,
# and possible data quality concerns requiring further attention.
#
# I am also reviewing the characteristics of temporal and logical
# variables to assess their consistency with the transformations
# implemented during the preceding data-cleaning stages.
#
# By systematically examining these statistical summaries,
# I am developing a more nuanced understanding of the dataset's
# underlying composition before undertaking substantive analysis.
#
# This exploratory assessment is particularly important because
# Netflix engagement data may exhibit considerable heterogeneity
# across titles, reporting periods, and content durations.
#
# Ultimately, I am using this diagnostic procedure to strengthen
# the methodological rigor of my investigation, identify potential
# analytical limitations, and establish an empirical foundation
# for subsequent comparisons, visualizations, and interpretations.

library(skimr)

skim(NETFLIX_DATA)
```

### Interpretation of Exploratory Findings

The preliminary exploratory analysis reveals a dataset
comprising 61,892 observations and 11 variables, representing
24,427 distinct Netflix titles across seven semiannual
reporting periods between 2023 and 2026.

The distribution of audience engagement is markedly
right-skewed. Average viewing hours approximate 8.27 million,
substantially exceeding the median of 1.8 million.


## Task 5: Exploring Netflix Viewing Patterns


```{r}
#| label: task5-calculations

# Conducting Quantitative Analysis of Netflix Viewing Engagement
#
# In this section, I am performing a series of quantitative
# calculations to investigate the temporal coverage, content
# diversity, audience engagement, and global accessibility
# of Netflix's streaming catalog.
#
# I am leveraging the cleaned and standardized NETFLIX_DATA
# dataset to derive empirical measures that address the
# principal analytical questions in this mini-project.
#
# My approach combines temporal analysis, distinct-title
# enumeration, conditional filtering, aggregation, and
# proportional calculations to evaluate different dimensions
# of Netflix's content consumption patterns.
#
# I am also ensuring that missing observations are handled
# appropriately and that each calculation produces a clearly
# defined metric suitable for subsequent interpretation.


# Loading the Libraries Required for Quantitative Analysis
#
# I am loading tidyverse to facilitate data manipulation,
# conditional filtering, grouping, and statistical aggregation.
#
# I am also loading scales to support the formatting of
# numerical results, particularly percentages and large
# viewing-hour totals, during subsequent presentation.

library(tidyverse)
library(scales)


# Q1: Determining the Temporal Coverage of My Netflix Dataset
#
# I am identifying the earliest and latest reporting dates
# represented in my consolidated Netflix engagement dataset.
#
# Specifically, I am extracting the minimum period_start
# and maximum period_end values to establish the complete
# chronological boundaries of my investigation.
#
# This calculation allows me to determine the overall
# reporting window covered by the available observations.
#
# Establishing these temporal boundaries is essential for
# contextualizing subsequent longitudinal comparisons and
# ensuring that my interpretation of viewing trends reflects
# the actual reporting periods included in the dataset.
#
# I am storing these boundaries as start_date and end_date
# for convenient reference in subsequent analytical outputs.

start_date <- min(NETFLIX_DATA$period_start)

end_date <- max(NETFLIX_DATA$period_end)


# Q2: Calculating the Number of Distinct Netflix Titles
#
# I am determining the total number of unique content titles
# represented across all reporting periods in my dataset.
#
# Rather than counting every observation independently,
# I am using n_distinct() to identify unique title values,
# thereby avoiding repeated enumeration of titles appearing
# in multiple semiannual engagement reports.
#
# This distinction is important because an individual title
# may remain available and generate viewing activity across
# several reporting periods.
#
# By calculating the number of distinct titles, I am
# establishing a descriptive measure of the breadth
# of Netflix's reported content catalog.
#
# I am storing the resulting count in total_titles for
# subsequent reporting and interpretation.

total_titles <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  summarise(
    n = n_distinct(title)
  ) |>
  pull(n)


# Q3: Measuring Cumulative Engagement Across the Bridgerton Universe
#
# I am examining the aggregate viewing engagement associated
# with Netflix's Bridgerton franchise, including related
# programming such as Queen Charlotte.
#
# To capture these interconnected productions, I am applying
# a case-insensitive regular expression that identifies
# titles containing either "Bridgerton" or "Queen Charlotte".
#
# This approach allows me to consolidate viewing activity
# across the broader franchise rather than evaluating
# individual productions in isolation.
#
# After identifying the relevant observations, I am
# aggregating their reported viewing hours across all
# available semiannual reporting periods.
#
# I am excluding missing values from the summation to
# prevent incomplete observations from interfering
# with the calculation.
#
# This metric provides an empirical measure of cumulative
# audience engagement associated with the franchise
# throughout the reporting window.
#
# I am storing the resulting value in bridgerton_hours
# for subsequent comparison with other major Netflix titles.

bridgerton_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(
    str_detect(
      title,
      regex(
        "Bridgerton|Queen Charlotte",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      )
    )
  ) |>
  summarise(
    total = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  pull(total)


# Q4: Calculating Stranger Things Viewing Hours
#     While Excluding Companion and Related Content
#
# I am investigating the cumulative viewing engagement
# associated with the primary Stranger Things series.
#
# Initially, I am identifying all observations containing
# "Stranger Things" within their titles using a
# case-insensitive regular expression.
#
# However, I recognize that matching titles may include
# companion programming, supplementary productions,
# or other related content that does not directly represent
# the principal television series.
#
# To improve the specificity of my calculation, I am
# applying an additional exclusion criterion to remove
# titles associated with Beyond Stranger Things,
# Tales from '85, and Fireplace content.
#
# This two-stage filtering process allows me to isolate
# a more narrowly defined subset of franchise-related
# observations for analytical comparison.
#
# Following these exclusions, I am summing the reported
# viewing hours across the available reporting periods.
#
# I am also accounting for missing values during aggregation
# to preserve the numerical validity of the resulting total.
#
# This calculation enables me to evaluate the cumulative
# engagement associated with the selected Stranger Things
# content without including the explicitly excluded
# companion productions.
#
# I am storing the resulting measure in
# stranger_things_hours for subsequent interpretation.

stranger_things_hours <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(
    str_detect(
      title,
      regex(
        "Stranger Things",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      )
    )
  ) |>
  filter(
    !str_detect(
      title,
      regex(
        "Beyond Stranger Things|Tales from.?85|Fireplace",
        ignore_case = TRUE
      )
    )
  ) |>
  summarise(
    total = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  pull(total)


# Q5: Evaluating Viewing Concentration Among the
#     Ten Most-Watched Titles in the First Half of 2026
#
# I am examining the extent to which Netflix viewing
# engagement was concentrated among its ten most-watched
# titles during the 2026H1 reporting period.
#
# First, I am restricting my dataset to observations
# associated with the first half of 2026.
#
# I am then grouping the observations by title and
# aggregating their reported viewing hours to establish
# a comparable measure of audience engagement.
#
# Next, I am arranging the titles in descending order
# of total viewing hours to identify the ten titles
# generating the greatest aggregate engagement.
#
# I am calculating the combined viewing hours of these
# ten titles and dividing that figure by the total
# viewing hours recorded during the same reporting period.
#
# This proportional measure allows me to assess the
# concentration of audience attention within a relatively
# small subset of Netflix's reported content catalog.
#
# A higher percentage would indicate that viewing activity
# is disproportionately concentrated among leading titles,
# whereas a lower percentage would suggest a more
# distributed pattern of content consumption.
#
# I am storing this proportion in top10_share for
# subsequent percentage formatting and interpretation.

top10_share <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(period == "2026H1") |>
  group_by(title) |>
  summarise(
    hours = sum(hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(hours)) |>
  summarise(
    share = sum(head(hours, 10)) / sum(hours)
  ) |>
  pull(share)


# Q6: Measuring Global Availability Across
#     Netflix Title-Period Observations
#
# I am evaluating the proportion of Netflix title-period
# observations classified as globally available.
#
# Because the same title may appear in multiple reporting
# periods, I am treating each title-period observation
# as a separate record in this calculation.
#
# First, I am excluding observations with missing
# global-availability classifications to ensure that
# the denominator contains only records for which
# availability status is known.
#
# I am then calculating the arithmetic mean of the
# available_globally logical variable.
#
# Since I previously converted this variable into
# Boolean format, TRUE values are interpreted as 1
# and FALSE values as 0 during numerical aggregation.
#
# Consequently, the resulting mean represents the
# proportion of nonmissing title-period observations
# designated as globally available.
#
# This calculation provides an unweighted measure
# of global content accessibility, with each eligible
# observation contributing equally regardless of
# its audience engagement.
#
# I am storing the resulting proportion in
# global_title_share for subsequent comparison.

global_title_share <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(!is.na(available_globally)) |>
  summarise(
    share = mean(available_globally)
  ) |>
  pull(share)


# Q6: Measuring Global Availability Weighted
#     by Total Viewing Hours
#
# I am extending my analysis of global availability
# by incorporating the relative viewing engagement
# associated with each title-period observation.
#
# Unlike the preceding calculation, which assigns
# equal importance to every eligible observation,
# this approach weights global availability according
# to the number of viewing hours generated.
#
# First, I am excluding observations with missing
# availability classifications to maintain consistency
# between the numerator and denominator.
#
# I am then calculating the aggregate viewing hours
# associated with globally available content.
#
# Next, I am dividing this amount by the total
# viewing hours across all observations with
# known global-availability status.
#
# This calculation produces the proportion of
# reported viewing hours attributable to content
# classified as globally available.
#
# By comparing this engagement-weighted proportion
# with the unweighted title-period proportion,
# I am investigating whether globally available
# content accounts for a disproportionately large
# or small share of Netflix viewing activity.
#
# This distinction is analytically important because
# content availability and audience engagement
# represent related but fundamentally different
# dimensions of Netflix's streaming ecosystem.
#
# I am storing the resulting proportion in
# global_hours_share for subsequent comparative analysis.

global_hours_share <- NETFLIX_DATA |>
  filter(!is.na(available_globally)) |>
  summarise(
    share = sum(hours_viewed[available_globally]) /
            sum(hours_viewed)
  ) |>
  pull(share)

```

### 5.1 Temporal Coverage

The Netflix viewing dataset covers the period from
`r format(start_date, "%B %d, %Y")` through
`r format(end_date, "%B %d, %Y")`, encompassing seven
semiannual reporting periods.

### 5.2 Content Diversity

The dataset contains `r scales::comma(total_titles)`
distinct titles, reflecting the breadth of Netflix's
programming catalog across the observation period.

### 5.3 The Bridgerton Universe

Content associated with the Bridgerton franchise,
including Queen Charlotte, accumulated approximately
`r scales::comma(bridgerton_hours)` viewing hours
across the reporting periods.

### 5.4 Stranger Things Franchise

The five seasons of Stranger Things collectively generated
approximately `r scales::comma(stranger_things_hours)`
viewing hours. This calculation excludes companion
productions and related background entertainment.

### 5.5 Audience Concentration in 2026H1

During the first half of 2026, the ten most-watched
titles accounted for `r scales::percent(top10_share,
accuracy = 0.01)` of total viewing hours.

This statistic provides an indication of the extent
to which audience engagement is concentrated among
Netflix's most successful titles.

### 5.6 Global Content Availability

Among title-period observations with known availability,
`r scales::percent(global_title_share, accuracy = 0.01)`
were classified as globally available.

When weighted by total viewing hours, globally available
content represented `r scales::percent(global_hours_share,
accuracy = 0.01)` of viewing activity associated with
records having known availability.

The distinction between catalog representation and
viewership-weighted availability helps assess whether
globally distributed programming attracts a
disproportionate share of audience engagement.
